title: Gender parity in schooling is advancing across generations, but attainment, learning, and opportunity are diverging
source_unit: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11455, Convergence or Reversal? The Evolution of the Gender Gap in Education in Sub-Saharan Africa
geography: Sub-Saharan Africa; microdata from Demographic and Health Surveys and Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys covering 35 countries, supplemented by learning assessments in 14 francophone countries

observations.period: Birth cohorts from the 1970s through cohorts born after 1999; educational attainment

denominator.unit: approximately individuals across 35 Sub-Saharan African countries in DHS/MICS microdata

historical_gap.value: among cohorts born in the 1970s, female disadvantage was approximately 13–15 percentage points in primary and secondary attendance and about 1.9 years of schooling

cohort_convergence.value: attainment gaps narrow sharply across cohorts and are statistically insignificant across most youngest birth cohorts

youngest_cohorts.value: among people born after 1999, females exceed males in secondary attendance and years of education in a majority of countries

mechanism.value: regional gender convergence is a generational process rather than a uniform contemporaneous improvement across all places and education stages

observations.method: Cross-cohort descriptive analysis of harmonized DHS and MICS microdata from 35 countries, with country-specific education-cycle and demographic controls.
observations.uncertainty: Cohort comparisons are descriptive and can reflect selection, survey timing, school expansion, migration, mortality, and country-specific changes rather than a single causal intervention.
observations.subgroup: Girls and boys across birth cohorts, primary and secondary attendance, countries, rural and urban populations, and socioeconomic and religious groups.
observations.counterinterpretation: Apparent parity can coexist with low absolute attendance, changing male participation, selective survival or migration, and unequal school quality; attendance is not the same as learning or later opportunity.

observations.period: Birth cohorts and learning assessments; attainment versus learning

denominator.unit: francophone Sub-Saharan African countries with international educational assessment and monitoring data

learning_direction.value: learning gaps show no uniform direction across countries and often run counter to attainment gaps

conversion_gap.value: more equal attendance does not guarantee more equal measured learning

institutional_signal.value: gender parity metrics can conceal differences in instructional quality, completion, subject pathways, and usable skills

work_route.value: education parity may improve future work options only when schooling converts into learning, credentials, mobility, and non-discriminatory labor-market opportunity

observations.method: Supplementary analysis using international assessment and monitoring data for 14 francophone countries, compared with attainment patterns.
observations.uncertainty: Learning measures, assessments, grade levels, language, cohorts, and country coverage differ from the household-survey attainment data; the study does not estimate labor-market or income effects.
observations.subgroup: Girls and boys in assessed countries, school systems with different language and quality conditions, and learners whose attendance does or does not translate into measured competencies.
observations.counterinterpretation: Assessment differences may reflect curriculum, test design, language, participation, or school selection rather than a stable gender learning disadvantage.

observations.period: Young and recent birth cohorts; persistent subgroup inequality

denominator.unit: Sub-Saharan African countries in the regional attainment analysis

persistent_gaps.value: wider attainment gaps persist among rural, poorer, and Muslim populations

unequal_convergence.value: regional and aggregate convergence can coexist with persistent exclusion for groups facing distance, poverty, gender norms, school costs, insecurity, or weaker supply

generational_meaning.value: younger women's educational gains can change family expectations and future agency while leaving place- and class-specific constraints intact

next_outcome.value: the open question is whether parity converts into learning, employment, earnings, voice, health, delayed marriage, and household bargaining power

observations.method: Subgroup comparison across country, rurality, wealth, and religious-population patterns in harmonized survey data.
observations.uncertainty: The study documents associations and cohort patterns, not the causal contribution of poverty, rural residence, religion, school supply, household preferences, safety, or labor-market discrimination.
observations.subgroup: Rural households, poorer households, Muslim populations, girls and boys, younger cohorts, and countries with different education systems and social norms.
observations.counterinterpretation: Persistent gaps may partly reflect differences in survey measurement, population composition, school-cycle definitions, or the timing of reforms; subgroup patterns should not be read as cultural essentialism.

related_sources.claim: Bibliographic record and abstract for WPS11455, including sample, cohort convergence, learning divergence, and subgroup patterns.
World Bank reproducibility package describing DHS, MICS, PASEC, and harmonized learning data, access conditions, and reproduction materials.

boundary: This record adds generational education convergence with a measurement and conversion gap between attendance, learning, work, and agency. It is descriptive cohort evidence, not a causal evaluation of schooling reform, current prevalence estimate, or proof that educational parity has already produced equal labor-market, household, health, or political outcomes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official World Bank PDF, abstract record, and reproducibility metadata were reviewed for the 35-country and approximately 736,000-person microdata frame, cohort attainment gaps, post-1999 reversal pattern, 14-country learning-assessment comparison, persistent rural/poor/Muslim subgroup gaps, and data-access boundaries.
